title: A century-old machine plays three real violins, using just one string on each

cover.alt: The 1912 Phonoliszt-Violina at the Deutsches Museum: a carved wooden cabinet with three violins inside a ring-shaped bow above a paper music roll and a piano keyboard.

body: The Hupfeld Phonoliszt-Violina, from the German firm of Ludwig Hupfeld in Leipzig, joined a self-playing piano to three violins. Bellows pressed each violin against a **circular bow**, and only one string on each violin sounded, its note set by mechanical ‘fingers’ that were also driven by bellows. Punched paper rolls controlled the violins, just as they controlled the piano. It was judged aesthetically unsatisfactory, yet by 1930 some 3,500 had been built.

slides.alt: Hand-held phone footage of a carved wooden cabinet: three violins sit inside a large ring-shaped bow, a paper roll turns in a window below them, and a piano keyboard and a ‘Phonoliszt Violina’ nameplate sit at the bottom.
slides.caption: The 1912 Phonoliszt-Violina at the Deutsches Museum in Munich plays itself: three violins inside a ring-shaped bow, the paper roll turning below them, and a self-playing piano.

right.label: The Violina
right.text: Pushes three violins against a ring-shaped bow; air-driven ‘fingers’ stop one string on each.

slides.label: Violinas built by 1930
slides.text: In the 1920s Hupfeld was the largest European maker of mechanical musical instruments.

slides.question: On each of the Violina’s three violins, how many strings actually play?
options: None: the piano plays the tune
slides.explanation: Just one string on each violin played, with its note set by ‘fingers’ driven by bellows, the same air power that pressed the violin against the bow.
